title: Design an Audio Streaming Service
summary: Hundreds of millions of small files with high-QPS random access and offline sync — the inverse storage shape of video's few-huge-files problem.

slides.markdown:
The prompt: stream any of hundreds of millions of songs instantly, on any device, plus let users download tracks for offline listening.

The catalog shape is the opposite of [design-video-streaming-platform](design-video-streaming-platform)'s: instead of few, huge files needing heavy transcoding, you have a vast number of small, cheap-to-store files needing very fast, very frequent metadata lookups. That shift moves the hard problem from transcode compute to catalog/metadata QPS.

**Functional:** stream a track instantly, download tracks for offline listening, sync playlists and playback position across a user's devices.

**Non-functional:** low startup latency (sub-second, since users skip tracks constantly), correct **offline license expiry** — a downloaded track must stop playing once its license lapses, even with zero connectivity to check in — and **gapless playback** between consecutive tracks on an album, which most video platforms don't need to solve at all.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: back-of-envelope — audio's storage shape vs video's
slides.markdown:
| | Audio catalog | Video catalog |
|---|---|---|
| Catalog size | Hundreds of millions of tracks | Millions of titles |
| Per-item storage | ~5-10MB per track (a few minutes, compressed) | Several GB per title across renditions |
| Concurrent streams | Very high — tens of millions, each a tiny stream | Lower count, but each stream is far heavier |
| Total catalog bytes | Large from sheer item count | Large from per-item size |

Even though total catalog bytes can land in a similar ballpark, audio gets there via item *count*, not item *size* — which is why audio's bottleneck shows up in lookups per second, while video's shows up in bytes per second.

`getStreamUrl(trackId)` returns a short-lived, signed URL to the track's audio object — resolved fast, since a skip-heavy listening session calls this constantly. `download(trackId)` issues a license-bound copy for offline playback, tied to an expiry the client must enforce locally.

Cross-device **playlist and playback-position sync** is its own call pattern: a background sync endpoint that reconciles a user's playlists and "resume from here" position across whichever device they open next, independent of which device was streaming last.

slides.sectionTitle: Data model: small immutable audio objects plus a metadata/catalog service
slides.markdown:
Each track's audio bytes are stored once as an immutable object (a track's audio never changes after ingestion, unlike a video that might get re-transcoded). Because these objects are small and numerous, the system leans harder on a **metadata/catalog service** — title, artist, album, licensing region, and the pointer to the audio object — than a video system does, since nearly every user action starts with a catalog lookup.

This catalog service is the one most likely to need aggressive caching and read replicas, since its query volume tracks skip and search behavior, not just stream starts.

![Client querying catalog metadata, then fetching audio bytes through a CDN-fronted object store](assets/audio-catalog-vs-bytes.svg)

Notice the catalog lookup and the audio-byte fetch are two separate hops through two differently-shaped systems — a small, hot, read-heavy metadata store, and a large, cold-by-default object store behind a CDN.

assets.alt: Client querying catalog metadata, then fetching audio bytes through a CDN-fronted object store

slides.sectionTitle: Offline downloads: syncing licensed content and expiring it without connectivity
slides.markdown:
A downloaded track ships to the device encrypted, with a **license object** stating an expiry (often tied to the user's subscription renewal cycle). The client enforces expiry locally — it must refuse to play an expired license even with no network to ask the server, which means the expiry check and the decryption key handling both have to live client-side, not just trust a server flag fetched at download time.

The server's job is periodically refreshing valid licenses while the subscription is active, and simply *not* refreshing them once it lapses — the device, not the server, is what stops playback.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: cross-device playlist and playback-position sync
slides.markdown:
![Phone pushes playback position to a sync service, laptop pulls it to resume at the same spot](assets/playback-sync-devices.svg)

The sync service only needs to hold small, frequently-overwritten state — current position, playlist order — so it's a very different read/write shape from either the catalog or the audio object store, and usually deserves its own storage tier.

assets.alt: Phone pushes playback position to a sync service, laptop pulls it to resume at the same spot

slides.sectionTitle: The bottleneck: metadata/catalog lookups at far higher QPS than video's per-title lookups
slides.markdown:
A video viewer typically picks one title and watches for tens of minutes, generating one manifest lookup per long session. An audio listener skips constantly — search, queue, skip, repeat — generating catalog lookups many times a minute per active user, across hundreds of millions of tracks.

That QPS gap is the actual bottleneck audio systems fight, not storage bytes: the catalog service needs heavy caching (hot tracks, trending searches) and horizontal read scaling far beyond what a comparable video metadata service would need for the same user count.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: pre-computing personalized playlists vs computing them on read
slides.markdown:
| | Pre-computed playlists | Computed on read |
|---|---|---|
| Freshness | Can lag behind the user's most recent listens | Always reflects the latest signals |
| Read latency | Very low — a simple lookup | Higher — ranking runs per request |
| Compute cost pattern | Paid once per user, on a schedule (e.g. nightly) | Paid on every playlist open |
| Personalization depth | Batch jobs can use heavier models offline | Must fit within request-latency budgets |

**How to decide:** pre-compute for playlists opened often by many users (a daily mix), and compute on read only for surfaces where the request volume is low enough or freshness matters enough to justify the per-request cost.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: treating audio like small video
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Audio is basically video with smaller files, so it needs the same rendition ladder and adaptive bitrate machinery."

**Why it's wrong:** a compressed audio track is only a few megabytes — well within a phone's cache or even RAM — so the multi-rendition, chunked-ABR complexity that video needs to survive a fluctuating network is mostly unnecessary overhead here; most players just fetch a couple of fixed bitrate options and buffer the whole track.

**Correct model:** size the design around audio's real bottleneck — catalog QPS and offline license handling — rather than importing video's ABR machinery wholesale just because both are "streaming."
